summary:
Same-sex conduct between adults was decriminalised by the High Court in Jones v Attorney General in 2018, a ruling upheld on appeal. The challenge was brought by the activist Jason Jones, who stated publicly during the proceedings that he faced up to 25 years' imprisonment for consensual sex with an adult male partner, the maximum exposure under the criminal provisions then in force. Decriminalisation removed the threat of prosecution without producing legal gender recognition.

Gender identity has no separate legal standing in Trinidad and Tobago. Rae Alibey, director of the Trinidad and Tobago Transgender Coalition, said in July 2024 that the trans community is the most marginalised group in the country and is not recognised in law: gender identity is not recognised separately from sexual orientation, and institutional forms carry no gender-identity markers.

Entry rules still carry the older prohibition. Section 8 of the Immigration Act bars homosexual men and women who are not citizens from entering Trinidad and Tobago, and the provision is not known to have been enforced. In 2016 the Caribbean Court of Justice held that neither Trinidad and Tobago nor Belize violated the freedom of movement of the Jamaican activist Maurice Tomlinson, while clarifying that neither state may bar homosexuals from CARICOM countries from entering, on the basis of treaty obligations under the Treaty of Chaguaramas.

There is no specific hate-crime category in the legislation, a gap identified by Supt Claire Guy-Alleyne in June 2024 while pointing to almost half a dozen Grindr-related attacks in recent months. In November 2024 the police warned that criminals create fake dating accounts to lure LGBT+ victims into meetings followed by armed robbery, beatings or sexual assault, with two separate incidents reported in a single week.

The PNM Constitution Review Committee rejected the addition of sexual-orientation protections to the national constitution, a decision announced at a special convention in August 2024. Dr Angelique Nixon of CAISO said the community has "been waiting far too long for equal rights and protection".

Partnership recognition is absent: Trinidad and Tobago does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same rights and benefits as opposite-sex households.

Custody and court practice stand under the "Justice through a Gender Lens" Gender Equality Protocol for Judicial Officers, launched in November 2018 by the Caribbean Court of Justice, CAJO, UN Women, the JURIST Project, TTAWJ and the Judicial Institute of Trinidad and Tobago. The Protocol states that there are no special facilities in the Trinidad and Tobago penal system to safely accommodate persons with non-traditional gender identities. It directs judicial officers sentencing a person whose gender identity does not accord with their birth certificate to make recommendations to prison authorities so that provisions are in place for the inmate's physical safety, and instructs courts to refer to intersex and transgender persons by their chosen pronoun and to permit court access irrespective of dress. Housing placement for a trans prisoner therefore rests on a discretionary sentencing recommendation, with no facility of its own.
tangentialFactors:
Official rhetoric on reform has been split. On 17 June 2016 Prime Minister Keith Rowley told Parliament that the state must protect all citizens "regardless of whom they sleep with", while refusing to repeal the same-sex criminal laws. That statement predates the 2018 decriminalisation ruling and records the reform-refusal position of the government of the day.

Attitudinal evidence in this inventory is old and measures sexual orientation rather than gender identity. A 2009 University of the West Indies study for the Ministry of Social Development found that four of every five Trinbagonians believed in denying someone rights or equality based on sexual orientation; the finding prompted the founding of CAISO to encourage public discussion and legislative protections. The survey window closed in 2009 and no later measurement of comparable attitudes appears in the sources.

Judicial handling of same-sex property disputes has been tested once in this record. In July 2018 Justice Frank Seepersad approved a property dispute resolution between two gay partners, noted unequal treatment under current law, and warned that without an agreement the court would have had to rely on innovative applications of trust law to determine property division after dissolution of a same-sex union.
localsOnly:
Same-sex couples are unable to legally adopt in Trinidad and Tobago, and households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same rights and benefits as opposite-sex households.

Resident-facing support machinery is thin and civil-society led. The Silver Lining Foundation works to end bullying against LGBTQ youth, and CAISO was founded to encourage public discussion and legislative protections after the 2009 attitudinal study.

The Gender Equality Protocol for Judicial Officers binds court practice for residents as well as visitors: it requires chosen pronouns and dress-based court access for intersex and transgender persons, and requires sentencing judges to make safety recommendations to prison authorities, since the penal system holds no facility designed for non-traditional gender identities.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: no source in this inventory documents whether Section 8 of the Immigration Act has been applied to any individual traveller, before or after the 2018 decriminalisation ruling. The record states only that the provision is not known to have been enforced.

Unresolved: the 2024 constitutional-review exclusion is recorded in terms of sexual orientation. Whether gender identity was separately proposed or separately rejected by the PNM Constitution Review Committee is not sourced here.

Not sourced: this inventory contains no trans-specific killing or violence figure for Trinidad and Tobago, so no comparison against the national homicide rate can be made, and none should be inferred from the Grindr-related incident counts, which are raw counts over unspecified periods.

The GlobalGayz profile of August 2012 states that homosexuality is illegal and that the laws are mostly ignored in practice. It predates the 2018 decriminalisation ruling, so its statement of the law does not reflect current law, and its enforcement claim is not dated to any period after 2012.

Not sourced: no procedure for legal gender recognition, and no pending legislation to create one, appears anywhere in this inventory.
